frictionVectors.title: European Gas Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Algeria retains strong control over hydrocarbons while using pipeline and LNG exports to preserve leverage with Europe. European pressure for supply diversification and faster renewable development could gradually reduce that leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara Spillover
frictionVectors.details: Algeria's rivalry with Morocco continues to shape Maghreb security, energy diplomacy, and regional infrastructure alignments. The dispute limits cross-border economic integration and raises the strategic value of external partnerships.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese Finance Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Angola is reducing dependence on Chinese oil-backed financing, but debt servicing and infrastructure obligations still constrain policy flexibility. Beijing remains influential through construction, commodities, and commercial networks.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Transit
frictionVectors.details: The Lobito Corridor is attracting US, European, and regional interest as an alternative route for copper and cobalt exports from the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Zambia. Angola gains transit leverage, but foreign competition may limit local value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel Militancy Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Insurgent spillover from Burkina Faso and Niger is increasing pressure on northern border communities and state logistics. Expanded security cooperation and border infrastructure risk drawing Benin deeper into competing regional and external security agendas.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Trade Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Cotonou remains central to Benin's revenue and regional trade, particularly with Nigeria and landlocked Sahel markets. Customs, corridor, and infrastructure dependence leaves the country vulnerable to policy shifts in larger neighboring economies.

frictionVectors.title: Diamond Market Concentration
frictionVectors.details: Botswana retains substantial influence over diamond extraction through its partnership with De Beers, but the government remains exposed to global demand, synthetic stones, and negotiations over value sharing. Processing and local beneficiation are key tests of sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: Water and Energy Constraints
frictionVectors.details: Water scarcity and dependence on regional electricity systems constrain mining expansion and industrial diversification. New resource projects could deepen pressure on aquifers and infrastructure unless domestic capacity improves.

frictionVectors.title: Gold Governance and Informal Mining
frictionVectors.details: Gold is the regime's principal strategic resource, but informal production, smuggling, and opaque security-linked networks limit public revenue capture. Efforts to increase state control may raise short-term sovereignty while weakening transparency and investor confidence.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security Alignment
frictionVectors.details: The junta's shift away from France and other Western partners toward Russia has increased geopolitical autonomy rhetoric but not resolved the security crisis. External security support, arms access, and mining interests risk becoming intertwined.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals governance
frictionVectors.details: The government is seeking greater control over nickel, rare-earth, and gold projects, but limited regulatory capacity and opaque licensing leave room for foreign and politically connected intermediaries.

frictionVectors.title: Rwanda border pressure
frictionVectors.details: Persistent accusations of support for armed proxies and cross-border insecurity complicate trade, security cooperation, and Burundi's ability to manage its own regional agenda.

highlights: Aid and tourism remain structural dependencies

frictionVectors.title: External control of strategic infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Port, airport, digital, and energy projects rely heavily on European, Chinese, and other external finance, creating long-term exposure despite generally strong state institutions.

frictionVectors.title: Maritime security burden
frictionVectors.details: Cabo Verde's location makes it valuable for anti-trafficking and Atlantic security operations, while limited naval capacity leaves enforcement dependent on foreign partners.

highlights: Oil, gas, timber, and minerals remain externally exposed

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon and timber concessions
frictionVectors.details: Foreign energy firms and logging interests retain substantial influence over production and infrastructure, while weak transparency limits domestic capture of resource rents.

frictionVectors.title: Anglophone conflict and transport corridors
frictionVectors.details: Insurgency in the Northwest and Southwest disrupts roads, plantations, and public authority, increasing dependence on security providers and undermining national infrastructure control.

highlights: Russian security partnership dominates sovereignty calculus
Gold and diamonds remain weakly governed

frictionVectors.title: Russian military and mining influence
frictionVectors.details: The government's security relationship with Russian personnel has reduced reliance on some Western actors but is tied to opaque access, political leverage, and protection of mining interests.

frictionVectors.title: Resource corridor insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Armed groups and cross-border networks continue to contest gold, diamonds, and transport routes, limiting the state's ability to tax production or secure infrastructure independently.

frictionVectors.title: Oil-sector dependency
frictionVectors.details: Chad remains reliant on foreign operators, export infrastructure, and external technical capital for oil production, leaving fiscal sovereignty vulnerable to price shifts and concession terms.

frictionVectors.title: Sudan border and foreign security ties
frictionVectors.details: War in Sudan strains refugee, trade, and border-management systems, while Chad's longstanding external security partnerships complicate efforts to build fully autonomous control over its territory.

frictionVectors.title: Mayotte and French Influence
frictionVectors.details: France retains control of Mayotte, sustaining a core territorial dispute and shaping Comoros migration, aid, and maritime policy. Moroni has limited leverage beyond diplomatic and regional pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Weak Maritime Resource Capacity
frictionVectors.details: Limited coast-guard, port, and fisheries capacity leaves Comoros dependent on external partners to police its maritime zone and develop blue-economy assets.

frictionVectors.title: Eastern Security and Regional Interference
frictionVectors.details: M23-linked instability and wider tensions involving Rwanda continue to weaken Kinshasa's control over territory, trade routes, and mineral zones. Regional diplomacy and external security backing remain central to the conflict.

frictionVectors.title: Cobalt and Copper Dependency
frictionVectors.details: Foreign firms and state-backed investors dominate financing, processing, and export logistics for strategic minerals. Kinshasa is seeking more local value addition, but infrastructure and governance constraints limit bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Concentration
frictionVectors.details: Public finances and export earnings remain heavily tied to hydrocarbons, leaving Brazzaville exposed to price cycles and negotiations with international energy partners.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure-for-Resource Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed roads, telecommunications, and other projects provide important state capacity but can deepen debt, procurement, and long-term resource-leverage concerns.

frictionVectors.title: External Control of Cocoa Value
frictionVectors.details: Côte d'Ivoire has strengthened regulation and is pursuing more domestic processing, but foreign traders, financiers, and processors still capture substantial value from the cocoa chain.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel Spillover and Port Security
frictionVectors.details: Instability from neighboring Sahel states raises costs for northern transport corridors and border security. Abidjan's port expansion also increases reliance on foreign capital, operators, and technology.

frictionVectors.title: Base and Port Competition
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti leverages its position at the Red Sea gateway to host foreign military facilities and manage strategic ports, but competing Chinese, American, French, and Gulf interests narrow policy autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Infrastructure Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Large port, rail, and logistics projects have expanded national connectivity while increasing exposure to debt restructuring, external operators, and strategic bargaining over infrastructure access.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and asset dependence
frictionVectors.details: Egypt relies heavily on IMF programs, Gulf deposits, and foreign investment while monetizing state assets and strategic land. This provides liquidity but narrows independent control over key infrastructure and revenue streams.

frictionVectors.title: Nile and Red Sea exposure
frictionVectors.details: The unresolved GERD dispute and instability around the Red Sea threaten Egypt's water security and Suez Canal earnings. Cairo is strengthening regional partnerships but has limited room for unilateral escalation.

frictionVectors.title: Mature oil and gas fields
frictionVectors.details: Falling production and limited new discoveries are reducing the state's resource rents. Foreign operators retain essential technical and commercial leverage as Malabo promotes gas processing and regional LNG cooperation.

frictionVectors.title: External capital concentration
frictionVectors.details: Infrastructure and energy projects remain dependent on a narrow group of foreign partners, including Asian, European, and Gulf-linked firms. This limits diversification and leaves public finances vulnerable to commodity and financing shocks.

frictionVectors.title: Regional militarization
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's position on the Red Sea gives it strategic leverage amid tensions involving Ethiopia, Sudan, and external naval powers. That leverage also increases exposure to sanctions, diplomatic isolation, and renewed conflict.

frictionVectors.title: Mining sovereignty dispute
frictionVectors.details: Gold, copper, and zinc projects provide hard currency but depend on foreign operators and opaque state-linked structures. Revenue control is centralized, while labor and governance concerns constrain broader national benefit.

frictionVectors.title: Economic dependence on South Africa
frictionVectors.details: Eswatini depends heavily on South African supply chains, customs arrangements, remittances, finance, and electricity networks. Any regional slowdown or political deterioration quickly constrains its policy autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure and fiscal constraints
frictionVectors.details: The kingdom needs external finance for energy, water, and transport upgrades while managing limited fiscal space. Reliance on concessional lenders and trade preferences creates leverage for outside partners without fully displacing state control.

frictionVectors.title: Nile diplomacy remains unresolved
frictionVectors.details: Ethiopia has strengthened control over the GERD and expanded domestic energy ambitions, but Egypt and Sudan still contest operating rules and data-sharing arrangements. The dispute remains a persistent risk to regional stability and export plans.

frictionVectors.title: External finance and corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring, IMF engagement, and infrastructure financing bring essential relief but increase leverage for creditors and strategic partners. Djibouti corridor dependence and competition over ports constrain Ethiopia's ability to convert economic scale into full logistical sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Capital and Contract Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The post-coup authorities are seeking greater state control over oil, manganese, and infrastructure concessions while remaining dependent on foreign investment and technical expertise.

frictionVectors.title: French Influence Recalibration
frictionVectors.details: Libreville is diversifying external partnerships, but longstanding French commercial and political ties remain embedded in strategic sectors.

frictionVectors.title: Senegal Border and Casamance Linkages
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia's geography makes it heavily reliant on Senegal for transport, trade corridors, and security cooperation, limiting independent strategic maneuver.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Access to Fisheries
frictionVectors.details: Industrial fishing and weak monitoring continue to raise concerns over offshore resource depletion, foreign access, and lost public revenue.

highlights: Gold and Oil Face Governance Pressure

frictionVectors.title: Mining Dependence and Illegal Gold Extraction
frictionVectors.details: Gold remains central to foreign-exchange stability, but illegal mining damages land and water while exposing regulatory weaknesses and community grievances.

frictionVectors.title: External Financing Constraints
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and IMF-linked reforms strengthen fiscal discipline but narrow policy space around energy, infrastructure, and strategic resource ownership.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled Mining Corridors
frictionVectors.details: Bauxite and iron-ore expansion is tied to foreign capital, railways, ports, and processing commitments, creating leverage for external partners over national infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Junta Legitimacy and Contract Risk
frictionVectors.details: The military-led political transition creates uncertainty over licensing, local-content enforcement, and whether resource revenues will translate into broad public benefits.

frictionVectors.title: Cashew Trade Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Heavy reliance on raw cashew exports leaves producers exposed to foreign buyers and weak domestic processing capacity, limiting value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Port, Security, and Transnational Trafficking
frictionVectors.details: Weak institutions and recurring political instability make transport infrastructure vulnerable to illicit networks and external influence, constraining effective control of national territory.

frictionVectors.title: External Debt Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Debt-service pressure limits Nairobi's policy room and increases reliance on multilateral lenders and bilateral creditors. Infrastructure and financing partnerships with China, Gulf states, and Western institutions remain strategically competitive.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Power Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Foreign participation in Mombasa logistics, renewable power, and transmission projects creates long-term influence over critical infrastructure. Kenya retains substantial regulatory capacity but faces pressure to balance competing investors.

frictionVectors.title: Water Transfer Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Lesotho's control over its highland water resources is constrained by dependence on South Africa for revenue, infrastructure, and market access. Delays and disputes around major transfer projects expose asymmetry in bilateral bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Textile and Energy Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: The textile sector remains exposed to external market preferences and foreign-owned supply chains, while energy development depends heavily on outside finance. Limited diversification reduces Maseru's leverage over investors and partners.

frictionVectors.title: Iron-Ore Concession Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Large mining agreements provide fiscal and infrastructure benefits but leave Liberia exposed to foreign operators, commodity cycles, and bargaining imbalances. Local value addition and revenue enforcement remain central sovereignty concerns.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Corridor Competition
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed control and rehabilitation of ports, railways, and mineral corridors could improve connectivity while embedding long-term commercial influence. Monrovia must balance investor demands with transparent procurement and national-access obligations.

frictionVectors.title: Oil Infrastructure Rivalry
frictionVectors.details: Competing political and armed networks continue to use oil fields, terminals, and the National Oil Corporation as leverage. Foreign buyers, contractors, and political patrons benefit from fragmented governance and uncertain production access.

frictionVectors.title: Mercenary and Base Influence
frictionVectors.details: External military, security, and intelligence partnerships continue to shape control of strategic facilities and transport routes. Libya's divided institutions limit its ability to set consistent sovereign conditions for foreign involvement.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Concentration
frictionVectors.details: Nickel, cobalt, graphite, and other mineral projects attract foreign capital but expose Madagascar to commodity volatility and limited domestic processing. Weak oversight and uneven benefit-sharing fuel concerns over strategic resource control.

frictionVectors.title: Ports and Energy Bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-funded ports, roads, and renewable-energy projects are increasingly important to export capacity and national connectivity. Financing gaps give external partners substantial influence over project terms and logistics priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Concession Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Uranium and emerging mineral projects rely heavily on foreign operators and financing, limiting Malawi's negotiating leverage. Contract transparency and local value addition remain politically sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Energy Infrastructure Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Chronic electricity shortages and dependence on imported fuel constrain industrial sovereignty. External lenders and development partners retain significant influence over grid rehabilitation and energy policy.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Bamako's reliance on Russian security assistance has displaced Western and multilateral partnerships while increasing exposure to opaque security and commercial arrangements.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Contract Confrontations
frictionVectors.details: The government is using revised mining rules and tax claims to seek a larger share of gold revenues, producing disputes with major foreign operators and raising operational uncertainty.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Gas Governance
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project offers Mauritania greater fiscal and geopolitical leverage, but dependence on foreign technical operators and cross-border coordination with Senegal limits full sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese and Gulf Infrastructure Competition
frictionVectors.details: Port, rail, renewable-energy, and mining investments from external partners are accelerating connectivity while creating long-term exposure to foreign financing, concessions, and strategic bargaining.

frictionVectors.title: Chagos and Diego Garcia Settlement
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius continues to pursue sovereignty over the Chagos Archipelago while the future operating arrangements for Diego Garcia remain strategically tied to the United Kingdom and United States.

frictionVectors.title: Indian Ocean Strategic Competition
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius benefits from Indian, Western, and Asian investment but must prevent port, communications, and maritime-security partnerships from eroding strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara Resource Contest
frictionVectors.details: Morocco maintains effective control and develops phosphate, fisheries, port, and renewable assets in the territory, while the Polisario Front and some international actors continue to challenge the legal and diplomatic basis of those activities.

frictionVectors.title: Water and Energy Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale desalination, renewable-energy, and green-hydrogen programs strengthen autonomy but require substantial foreign capital, technology, and imported equipment.

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado LNG corridor
frictionVectors.details: Insurgent violence still threatens the restart and expansion of gas projects. Mozambique relies heavily on foreign operators and external security support to secure the resource zone.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and project-finance dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large infrastructure and LNG revenues remain constrained by opaque contracting, debt exposure, and limited domestic control over capital-intensive projects.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of frontier energy
frictionVectors.details: International firms dominate offshore oil appraisal and much of the emerging green-hydrogen pipeline. Namibia is seeking stronger local-content, tax, and state-participation terms.

frictionVectors.title: Port and logistics competition
frictionVectors.details: Walvis Bay infrastructure is becoming strategically important for regional minerals and energy exports, increasing pressure from foreign investors and neighboring trade interests.

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and oil renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: Niamey is challenging longstanding French-linked arrangements while seeking greater state control over uranium and oil. Reduced Western engagement increases the risk of financing, technology, and export bottlenecks.

frictionVectors.title: Security dependence shift
frictionVectors.details: The withdrawal of Western forces and reliance on Russian-linked security assistance have increased strategic autonomy rhetorically but created new external influence over defense and infrastructure priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline and oil-theft crisis
frictionVectors.details: Militancy, crude theft, and weak infrastructure continue to reduce effective state control over petroleum production. International operators retain major technical and financial leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Refinery sovereignty versus import exposure
frictionVectors.details: The Dangote refinery improves domestic processing capacity, but feedstock access, foreign-exchange constraints, and fuel-market policy remain contested between state and commercial interests.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-mineral supply-chain scrutiny
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda’s role as a regional minerals hub faces sustained scrutiny over the origin and transit of coltan and other resources linked to eastern Democratic Republic of Congo. Western due-diligence rules and Congolese pressure threaten reputational and commercial access.

frictionVectors.title: Security partnerships and regional leverage
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda uses external military, aid, and investment relationships to reinforce strategic autonomy, while its regional security posture generates diplomatic friction and possible sanctions exposure.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Exploration Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Potential hydrocarbons remain commercially uncertain, while exploration depends heavily on foreign capital and technical operators. Weak institutional capacity limits São Tomé and Príncipe’s leverage over future licensing terms.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Maritime Security
frictionVectors.details: Plans to expand maritime infrastructure could increase connectivity but also deepen dependence on external financiers and contractors. Illegal fishing and Gulf of Guinea security risks continue to erode control over surrounding waters.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Contract Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The government is seeking greater domestic value capture from new offshore oil and gas projects while avoiding disruption to operators and production schedules. Fiscal constraints and opaque legacy commitments limit its negotiating room.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and External Financing
frictionVectors.details: High debt exposure and financing gaps constrain Dakar’s ability to direct resource revenues independently. Relations with the IMF, Gulf financiers, China, and Western investors will shape infrastructure and energy policy.

frictionVectors.title: Tuna and Maritime Resource Control
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles benefits from a valuable tuna economy but remains dependent on foreign fleets, access agreements, and external processing capacity. Maritime surveillance and enforcement are essential to prevent resource leakage.

frictionVectors.title: External Security Competition
frictionVectors.details: India, China, Gulf states, and Western partners compete for access and influence around ports, logistics, and maritime security. The government must preserve strategic autonomy while relying on outside infrastructure and tourism capital.

frictionVectors.title: Iron Ore and Mining Dependency
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore and other mineral projects generate export potential but leave fiscal and infrastructure outcomes dependent on foreign operators and commodity prices. Contract disputes, local content demands, and environmental concerns remain persistent pressure points.

frictionVectors.title: Freetown Infrastructure Financing
frictionVectors.details: Port, energy, and transport upgrades require external finance, increasing exposure to Chinese, Gulf, and Western commercial interests. Limited state capacity complicates transparent procurement and long-term control of strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: Somaliland and Ethiopian Access
frictionVectors.details: Disputes over Somaliland’s external security and port relationships continue to challenge Mogadishu’s territorial authority. Competing Turkish, Gulf, Ethiopian, and Western interests add pressure around ports and maritime jurisdiction.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Hydrocarbon Governance
frictionVectors.details: Offshore licensing and exploration could provide revenue but remain vulnerable to weak institutions, federal-regional disputes, and security risks. Foreign operators and political intermediaries may capture a disproportionate share unless revenue-sharing and oversight improve.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral-processing dependence
frictionVectors.details: South Africa retains strong control over mining assets but remains dependent on foreign capital, technology, and export markets. Efforts to capture more battery and industrial value are constrained by unreliable electricity and logistics.

frictionVectors.title: Port and rail degradation
frictionVectors.details: Freight bottlenecks at Transnet ports and railways reduce sovereign control over mineral exports and encourage private or foreign logistical alternatives. Chinese, Gulf, and Western firms compete for influence through infrastructure and mining partnerships.

highlights: Peace process tied to external mediation

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline dependence
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan's oil revenues depend on transit infrastructure through Sudan, leaving production vulnerable to conflict, pipeline disruption, and bargaining by external actors. Limited refining and transport capacity prevents meaningful domestic resource sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Competing external security influence
frictionVectors.details: Regional governments, international donors, and security partners retain major influence over ceasefire implementation and political negotiations. Fragmented armed power continues to divert resource revenues away from state-building.

frictionVectors.title: Gold and war financing
frictionVectors.details: Gold production and smuggling networks provide revenue to rival armed centers and attract competing regional and international buyers. Weak state oversight makes mineral wealth a driver of continued conflict rather than national development.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea infrastructure contest
frictionVectors.details: Port access, maritime facilities, and transport corridors around the Red Sea are strategically contested by regional powers. External military and commercial interests exploit Sudan's fragmentation while constraining unified control of critical infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is strengthening sovereign leverage through the Dar es Salaam port and inland transport links serving mineral-producing neighbors. Chinese, Gulf, and Western investors compete for influence over logistics, energy, and industrial projects.

frictionVectors.title: Gas and mining bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Negotiations over offshore gas, uranium, and critical minerals reflect a push for greater local processing and revenue capture. Regulatory uncertainty and investor demands remain a recurring source of friction.

frictionVectors.title: Port dependence and external finance
frictionVectors.details: The Port of Lomé gives Togo regional leverage but also exposes strategic infrastructure to foreign lenders, operators, and trading networks. Competition among Gulf, Chinese, European, and regional actors shapes the country's logistics policy.

frictionVectors.title: Phosphate-sector constraints
frictionVectors.details: Togo retains formal control over phosphate resources, yet aging infrastructure and limited domestic processing reduce the state's ability to capture full value. Fiscal and technical dependence on outside partners remains significant.

frictionVectors.title: European Migration Leverage
frictionVectors.details: European funding and cooperation on migration management give the EU significant influence over Tunisia's domestic and external policy choices. Disputes over returns, border enforcement, and human-rights safeguards remain persistent.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and Phosphate Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Tunisia remains exposed to imported energy and constrained investment in its phosphate sector, limiting sovereign control over key revenue streams. Reliance on Algeria and European partners is deepening as fiscal pressures restrict state capacity.

frictionVectors.title: EACOP Financing and Sanctions Pressure
frictionVectors.details: The oil pipeline and upstream projects are financed and operated through foreign-led consortia, leaving Uganda exposed to external lenders, insurers, and environmental campaigns. Western pressure has increased scrutiny of land acquisition, compensation, and project governance.

frictionVectors.title: Regional Export Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Uganda's future oil revenues depend on transit infrastructure through Tanzania and stable regional relations. This creates leverage for neighboring states and international energy companies over the timing and commercial terms of exports.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Mining Dominance
frictionVectors.details: Zambia is seeking greater state participation, local processing, and revenue transparency in copper and cobalt, but foreign firms still control much of the capital, technology, and export infrastructure. Contract renegotiations risk investor uncertainty while the government tries to capture more value.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-Service and Power Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and IMF-supported reforms are improving fiscal credibility but constrain public investment choices. Electricity shortages and dependence on regional power imports threaten mining output and increase vulnerability to external suppliers.

frictionVectors.title: Lithium and Platinum Control
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and other foreign investors remain central to Zimbabwe's lithium, platinum, and gold sectors, while domestic processing capacity remains limited. Export restrictions have improved bargaining leverage in some minerals but have not yet created reliable sovereign value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Financial Isolation
frictionVectors.details: Sanctions, restricted access to international finance, and persistent currency instability push the government toward opaque bilateral deals and resource-backed arrangements. These constraints weaken oversight and increase dependence on non-Western creditors and trading partners.
